newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian envoy backs Hun Sen - report.
newsitem.headline: Australian envoy backs Hun Sen - report.

text.p: Australia's ambassador to Cambodia has urged Canberra to back the new regime of the war-torn country's co-premier Hun Sen, saying supporting his ousted rival Prince Norodom Ranariddh would only prolong fighting in the nation, a newspaper reported on Sunday.

Ambassador Tony Kevin, in a leaked diplomatic cable, said Second Prime Minister Hun Sen was a democrat at heart and was seeking a stable government to replace his uneasy coalition with First Prime Minister Ranariddh, the Sydney-based Sun-Herald reported.
Kevin said if nations such as Australia and the United States backed Hun Sen, but continued to apply some pressure, open elections due next year could go ahead on schedule.
"Is this not better than getting back into the sterile game of propping up Ranariddh?," the newspaper quoted Kevin as saying in the cable.
"It seems to me that this would simply help to prolong the long war -- and for what?"

A Foreign Affairs Department official told Reuters that the government would not comment on reports of leaked cables. Defence Minister Ian McLachlan also refused to comment on the cable during a television interview on Sunday.
But McLachlan said the cabinet would consider Australia's attitude to Cambodia over the next few days.
"I haven't seen confirmation of that cable yet, and no doubt if it's true we'll get it in the next couple of days," he said.
Hun Sen, backed by troops loyal to him, ousted Ranariddh and grabbed control of the capital Phnom Penh after two days of fighting last weekend.

"I think Hun Sen is now trying to pull off what he has always wanted -- a more or less well-governed Cambodia under CPP (Cambodian People's Party) control, but legitimised by a reasonably free and fair election in May, 1998," the newspaper quoted Kevin as saying.

Hun Sen and Ranariddh, who heads the royalist FUNCINPEC party, formed their uneasy power-sharing coalition after U.N.-organised elections in May 1993 which Ranariddh won. The coalition began falling apart last year when Ranariddh demanded more power in the provinces.
The next election is scheduled for May 1998.
Australia has already warned that aid and military assistance could be cut unless constitutional rule is restored, and has started drawing major aid donors together to discuss a joint response.

Prime Minister John Howard on Tuesday said Hun Sen's military take-over was "revolutionary" and that the new regime was not the authorised government in Canberra's eyes, but added that Australia also had to be realistic.
